You don't need a title to lead. Mentoring a junior, delegating a task or running a good one-to-one are leadership skills you can practise from your current seat. This final chapter prepares you for the step up, and ends with a daily routine to keep everything going.
10.1  Mentoring a junior
Teach them to fish, patiently.
The situation
A new joiner keeps asking you basic questions.
What skilled people do
They make time, explain the 'why', share resources, ask questions instead of giving answers, and check in regularly.
Say it like this
'Good question. What do you think the first step might be?'
'Here's why we do it this way. Try it and I'll review.'
Avoid
Doing the work for them, showing impatience, or making them feel stupid.
Practise today
Offer a junior colleague 15 minutes this week to answer their questions.
Say it aloud
Good question, what do you think?
Here's why we do it this way.
Try it and I'll review.
10.2  Delegating well
Give the outcome, context and freedom.
The situation
You do everything yourself because it's faster.
What skilled people do
They explain the goal, deadline and quality bar, share context, agree check-ins and let the person choose the method.
Say it like this
'I'd like you to own the vendor analysis. The goal is to pick the top three by Friday. Here's last year's file for context. Shall we check in Wednesday?'
Avoid
Micromanaging, dumping tasks without context, or taking work back at the first problem.
Practise today
Delegate one task this week using: goal, deadline, context, check-in.
Say it aloud
I'd like you to own the vendor analysis.
The goal is the top three by Friday.
Shall we check in on Wednesday?
10.3  Recognising others
Specific praise motivates more than any speech.
The situation
Your team works hard, but appreciation is rare or generic.
What skilled people do
They praise specifically and promptly, in public when appropriate, and tell the person's manager.
Say it like this
'Anita, your quick reconciliation saved the client deadline. Thank you. I've let your manager know too.'
Avoid
Generic 'good job', praise only at year-end, or taking the credit yourself.
Practise today
Give one colleague specific, sincere recognition today.
Say it aloud
Your quick work saved the deadline.
Thank you, it made a real difference.
I've let your manager know too.
10.4  Leading without a title
Influence comes from behaviour, not designation.
The situation
You see problems but feel it's not your place to act.
What skilled people do
They take ownership of small improvements, rally others around shared goals, and keep their manager informed.
Say it like this
'I noticed our handover notes are inconsistent. I've drafted a simple template; could we try it for two weeks?'
Avoid
Waiting for permission for everything, or acting without informing others.
Practise today
Pick one small team problem and propose a simple fix this week.
Say it aloud
I noticed our handover notes are inconsistent.
I've drafted a simple template.
Could we try it for two weeks?
10.5  Working across cultures
Adapt your style to how others communicate.
The situation
You work with colleagues from other regions and misunderstandings happen.
What skilled people do
They learn cultural norms (directness, hierarchy, time), avoid idioms, confirm understanding in writing, and stay curious.
Say it like this
'Just to confirm, we agreed on Tuesday 10 am UK time for the review, correct?'
'How does your team usually prefer to receive feedback?'
Avoid
Assuming everyone thinks like you, heavy slang, or stereotyping.
Practise today
Ask a colleague from another region how their team prefers to communicate.
Say it aloud
Just to confirm, we agreed on Tuesday 10 am UK time.
How does your team prefer feedback?
Please let me know if anything was unclear.
10.6  Leading remote and hybrid teams
Over-communicate and include everyone.
The situation
Remote colleagues feel left out of decisions made in the office.
What skilled people do
They document decisions, set clear norms (response times, cameras), run inclusive meetings and check in one-to-one.
Say it like this
'Let's hear from those online first.'
'I'll post the decision and next steps in the team channel.'
Avoid
Corridor decisions, ignoring people on calls, or measuring presence instead of output.
Practise today
In your next hybrid meeting, invite remote participants to speak first.
Say it aloud
Let's hear from those online first.
I'll post the decision in the team channel.
Does anyone joining remotely have thoughts?
10.7  Running effective one-to-ones
Their meeting, their agenda.
The situation
Your one-to-ones turn into status updates only.
What skilled people do
They let the other person set the agenda, ask open questions about goals and blockers, and follow up on commitments.
Say it like this
'What's on your mind this week?'
'What's one thing I could do to make your work easier?'
Avoid
Cancelling often, talking most of the time, or only discussing tasks.
Practise today
In your next one-to-one, ask 'What could I do to make your work easier?'
Say it aloud
What's on your mind this week?
What's getting in your way?
What could I do to make your work easier?
10.8  Handling underperformance
Address it early, kindly and clearly.
The situation
A team member's work keeps slipping and you avoid the conversation.
What skilled people do
They raise it early in private, use specific examples, listen for causes, agree clear expectations and offer support.
Say it like this
'I've noticed the last three reports were late. Is something getting in the way? Let's agree what on time looks like and how I can help.'
Avoid
Waiting until appraisal time, public criticism, or vague hints.
Practise today
If someone's work is slipping, plan a private, specific conversation using SBI.
Say it aloud
I've noticed the last three reports were late.
Is something getting in the way?
How can I help?
10.9  Building trust in a team
Trust = reliability + honesty + care.
The situation
Your team works in silos and hides problems.
What skilled people do
They keep promises, admit their own mistakes first, share information openly and show care for people.
Say it like this
'I got that wrong last week; here's what I learned.'
'It's fine to raise problems early; I'd rather know.'
Avoid
Punishing bad news, playing favourites, or inconsistency.
Practise today
Share one mistake you made and what you learned at your next team meeting.
Say it aloud
I got that wrong last week.
Here's what I learned.
Please raise problems early, I'd rather know.
10.10  Your daily people-skills routine
Small daily habits compound into a reputation.
The situation
You've learned many skills, but you need to practise them every day.
What skilled people do
They follow a simple routine: greet people by name, listen fully in one conversation, send one clear update, give one specific thank-you, and reflect for two minutes at day's end.

Trying to change everything at once, or giving up after one bad day.

Start the routine today and write a two-line reflection tonight: what went well, what to try tomorrow.
Say it aloud
Good morning, how was your weekend?
Quick update, the draft is ready for review.
Thanks, your help today made a difference.
